Consult Summary:
- 32-year-old man with 1–2 months of recurrent, transient right-sided hand paresthesia and right arm weakness with intermittent concurrent leg/gait weakness; GP referral made for urgent TIA clinic evaluation to exclude transient ischemic attack.

History:
- Presenting complaint and timeline:
  - Recurrent episodes (~1–2 months) of right-hand pins-and-needles and episodic right arm weakness; associated transient right leg weakness/abnormal gait reported by colleague.
  - Episodes initially monthly, now increasing to multiple times per day; each episode lasts a few days and then resolves completely.
  - Over the last few days patient noted transient difficulty holding a cup during episodes.
  - Also reports fatigue and intermittent nausea. Sensation of “something in my throat” during episodes.
  - Asymptomatic at time of teleconsultation.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - No current swallowing difficulty (denies ongoing dysphagia).
  - No speech disturbance reported.
  - No visual disturbance reported (wears glasses).
  - No headache reported in consultation.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No ongoing focal deficit on assessment.
  - No prior strokes/TIAs reported in patient.
  - No recent infection, neck pain, or systemic symptoms elicited.
- Past medical history, allergies, medications:
  - No chronic medical diagnoses reported; prior screening for BP, cholesterol, diabetes reportedly normal.
  - Medications: aspirin self-started 75 mg once daily (patient-initiated, not prescribed).
  - Allergy: penicillin.
- Social and preventive health factors:
  - Occupation: physician (plastic surgery).
  - Lives with wife; non-smoker.
  - Family history: father underwent carotid procedure (carotid endarterectomy) for stroke risk.

Examination:
- Vitals: none recorded in transcript.
- General/neurological exam: no objective neurological findings documented; patient asymptomatic during consult. No in-person exam possible (teleconsultation; video lost during encounter).
- Other observed findings: none recorded.

Impression:
- Working clinical impression (per clinician): Suspected transient ischemic attack (TIA) / mini-stroke — urgent exclusion required.
  - Transcript evidence: lateralized, transient sensory and motor deficits (right hand/arm ± leg), progressive increase in episode frequency, family history of carotid disease; GP explicitly stated presumptive diagnosis = TIA and arranged urgent TIA clinic referral.
- Additional leading differential considerations (DDx summary consistent with clinical features):
  1. Multiple sclerosis (relapsing–remitting demyelinating disease) — plausible/high on DDx:
     - Rationale: young adult with relapsing-remitting unilateral sensory and motor deficits lasting days with full recovery and associated fatigue; this pattern is characteristic for demyelinating events (noted in DDx).
     - Opposing: no prior documented episodes before this timeframe and no imaging/MC evidence yet.
  2. Hemiplegic (complex) migraine — possible/medium likelihood:
     - Rationale: episodic unilateral sensory and motor phenomena with nausea could represent migrainous aura; absence of reported headache and atypical frequency are opposing points.
  3. Recurrent TIAs from vascular cause — considered urgent by clinician/medium likelihood:
     - Rationale: lateralized transient deficits and family history prompted TIA clinic referral; however, typical TIAs are shorter (minutes–hours), whereas these episodes last days.
- Conflict noted:
  - Transcript (clinician) prioritized TIA and arranged urgent TIA clinic referral. The DDx algorithm ranked multiple sclerosis as the highest likelihood diagnosis. Conflict noted between clinician working diagnosis (TIA) and DDx highest-ranked diagnosis (MS). Transcript facts prioritized per instructions.

Plan:
- Immediate actions from consult (documented in transcript):
  - Urgent referral sent to local TIA / mini-stroke clinic; expected contact within 1–2 days (GP to send referral and include TIA clinic / PALS contact details in notes).
  - Patient advised to call the hospital/TIA clinic to confirm booking if desired (GP provided TIA clinic contact to be placed in notes).
  - Safety advice: if symptoms recur and persist/prolong (i.e., do not resolve or are prolonged), patient advised to attend A&E immediately (possible stroke).
  - If symptoms recur but are transient, patient may contact GP for telephone assessment and guidance.
- Investigations likely/anticipated by TIA clinic (as discussed in consult):
  - Carotid ultrasound (duplex) and brain imaging (CT or MRI as clinically indicated) — clinic to arrange.
- Medication / other immediate management:
  - No new prescriptions or medication changes documented in consult. (Patient is taking aspirin 75 mg daily by his own initiative; clinician discussed this but did not document stopping or changing it.)
  - Action item: ensure treating teams are aware patient self-started aspirin 75 mg daily (documented in chart / referral).
- Contingent recommendations consistent with DDx (to be considered if TIA is excluded):
  - If TIA/vascular causes are excluded by TIA clinic imaging and assessment, consider neurology referral and MRI brain (and spine if indicated) to evaluate for demyelinating disease (MS) or other structural/inflammatory causes — recommendation derived from DDx reasoning and should be acted on by neurology/TIA teams as appropriate.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No documented vital signs during consultation.
  - No focused neurological examination findings recorded (e.g., cranial nerve, motor power, tone, reflexes, coordination, sensory exam).
  - Exact date of birth not captured (age recorded as 32).
  - No history of headache timing/character (important for migraine differential) documented.
  - No detailed timeline of individual episode duration in hours vs days for every episode beyond “a few days.”
  - No prior imaging or investigations (dates/results) documented beyond patient-reported prior cardiovascular screening.
  - No explicit instruction documented regarding the patient-initiated aspirin (whether to continue or stop).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - Transcript clinician working diagnosis = TIA and referral to TIA clinic. DDx highest-ranked diagnosis = multiple sclerosis (relapsing–remitting) per reasoning system. Conflict noted.
- Transcript quality comment:
  - Teleconsultation with intermittent audio/connection issues; video was lost and not available for assessment. Patient was asymptomatic at time of consult so no examination could be performed. Overall history gathering was adequate but limited by lack of objective exam and imperfect connection; further in-person or face-to-face neurological assessment and urgent imaging are appropriate.
